prompt: A formatter rewrote 22 lines of a module. How many of the linter's four findings changed?
hint: Think about what each tool looks at.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Layout is not evidence. A finding that moved when the file was reformatted would be a finding about the formatting.

choices.text: Two — the ones about whitespace, which the formatter settled on its way through
choices.why: Whitespace rules are turned off precisely so this cannot happen.

choices.text: All four, since the line numbers moved and each finding is anchored to one
choices.why: The findings are re-derived from the new file and still name the same four things.

choices.text: One — the unused import, which the formatter removed while tidying the block
choices.why: A formatter removes nothing; deleting an import changes what the program does.

prompt: Why turn `E501` off when a formatter is in use?
hint: Who decided the line width?

choices.text: `E501` has no automatic fix, so every finding needs a person
choices.why: Neither does `E722`, and that one stays on.

choices.text: `E501` counts characters rather than display columns, so it is wrong about tabs
choices.why: It counts characters and that is not the objection here.

choices.text: A formatter emits lines longer than the limit whenever a string cannot be split
choices.why: That is a real and narrow case, and not the general reason.

choices.text: The formatter already chose the width, so a report about it is a report about the formatter's decision
choices.why: Let the formatter win on layout and keep the linter's rules that are about meaning.

prompt: Which of these is a formatter's decision and not a linter's?
hint: One has no right answer.

choices.text: Whether an import at the top of the file is used anywhere below
choices.why: That is a fact about the program and belongs to the linter.

choices.text: Whether a default argument is a list that outlives the call
choices.why: That is a defect and no formatter touches it.

choices.text: Whether a long call is written on one line or one argument per line
choices.why: There is no right answer to it, which is exactly why handing it to a program costs nothing.

choices.text: Whether a `try` block catches every exception or a named one
choices.why: That has a right answer, so it is reported rather than rewritten.

prompt: `ruff format` and `black` were run over the same module. What came out?
hint: It was measured with `diff`.

choices.text: The same bytes
choices.why: That is the claim `ruff format` makes, and it is one you can check on your own code before switching.

choices.text: The same layout with different quote characters on the string literals
choices.why: Both normalise to double quotes.

choices.text: Output that differs on long calls, where the two wrap differently
choices.why: They wrapped the long call identically here.

choices.text: Output that differs in blank lines around definitions at the top level
choices.why: The blank lines were the same.

prompt: What does a formatter change and a linter not?
hint: One of the two writes to the file.

choices.text: The bytes of the file
choices.why: A linter reports and changes nothing unless you ask it to with `--fix`.

choices.text: The meaning of the program, in the narrow cases where a rewrite is safe
choices.why: A formatter is not allowed to change meaning at all.

choices.text: The order of the imports, which is a layout question like any other
choices.why: Import order is `ruff`'s `I` family, on the linter's side.

choices.text: The set of names the module exports, when an unused one is removed
choices.why: Removing an import is a linter's `--fix`.

prompt: `black` reformatted a file and left `if result.ok == True:` exactly as it was. Why?
hint: Which tool has an opinion about that?

choices.text: `== True` is already formatted correctly, with the spaces `black` would put there
choices.why: It removed the space before the `:` on that very line, so it did touch it.

choices.text: A comparison to `True` is a linter's finding and a formatter has no opinion about it
choices.why: `E712` reports it. Rewriting it could change behaviour, which a formatter may never do.

choices.text: It is inside an `if`, and `black` leaves whole conditions alone to avoid changing branches
choices.why: It reformats conditions freely; what it will not do is change what one means.

choices.text: `black` skips any line that a linter rule already covers
choices.why: It knows nothing about the linter's rules.

prompt: What is the argument for `black` having almost no options?
hint: Think about what the options would be used for.

choices.text: Fewer options means a smaller program, which is why it runs as fast as it does
choices.why: Speed comes from the implementation rather than from the size of the option list.

choices.text: A formatter with settings is one a team can argue about, and removing the argument is the product
choices.why: `88` is a strange number and it is the default, which is the only property of it that matters.

choices.text: Each option would double the number of layouts the test suite has to cover
choices.why: That is a cost to its authors and not the reason given for the design.

choices.text: Options would make the output depend on a config file that may not be committed
choices.why: It reads `pyproject.toml`, which is committed like anything else.

prompt: You leave a trailing comma inside a call that would fit on one line. What does `black` do?
hint: The comma is a message.

choices.text: It keeps the comma and the single line, since both are valid
choices.why: The comma is read as a request to explode.

choices.text: It reports the comma as redundant and leaves the layout alone
choices.why: It reports nothing; it is a formatter.

choices.text: It removes the comma and joins the call onto one line
choices.why: It removes the comma only when the call is already on one line.

choices.text: It keeps the call exploded, one argument per line, with the comma still there
choices.why: The magic trailing comma is the one place you get to overrule it, and it is useful for a list that will grow.

prompt: Fail the build when a file is not formatted, and rewrite nothing: `black --______ app/`
hint: Five letters.

prompt: The first `black` run rewrites the whole repository. What goes with that commit?
hint: Think about `git blame` the week after.

choices.text: Its hash in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`, with `blame.ignoreRevsFile` pointed at the file
choices.why: Otherwise `git blame` answers 'the formatting commit' for every line in the project.

choices.text: A `.gitattributes` entry marking the reformatted files as generated
choices.why: That changes how diffs are displayed and does nothing for `blame`.

choices.text: A revert commit prepared in advance, in case the reformat broke something
choices.why: A formatter does not change behaviour, so there is nothing to revert.

choices.text: A tag, so the release before the reformat can still be built
choices.why: The reformat does not affect whether an older commit builds.

prompt: `[*] 3 fixable with the --fix option (1 hidden fix can be enabled with --unsafe-fixes)`. What is the hidden one?
hint: Think about what a fix is allowed to change.

choices.text: A fix that `ruff` cannot prove leaves the program's behaviour unchanged
choices.why: `result.ok == True` becoming `result.ok` is the example: `1 == True` is true and `1` is not `True`.

choices.text: A fix for a rule that is not in the selected set, which would be applied silently
choices.why: A rule that is not selected produces no finding to fix at all.

choices.text: A fix that would conflict with another fix on the same line
choices.why: Conflicting fixes are applied over several passes rather than hidden.

choices.text: A fix that rewrites more than one file, which needs the flag to be allowed
choices.why: Every fix here is within one file.

prompt: Which family holds most of the findings that are actual defects?
hint: It is named after an insect.

choices.why: flake8-bugbear: mutable defaults, a loop variable captured by a closure, an `assert` on a tuple.

choices.text: `E`, which is pycodestyle and is the largest family by rule count
choices.why: It is about whitespace and layout, which a formatter now owns.

choices.text: `SIM`, which finds code that could be written more directly
choices.why: Those are simplifications and the code they name is correct.

choices.text: `UP`, which rewrites syntax older than the target version
choices.why: Old syntax still runs; it is tidiness with a deadline.

prompt: What should you run first on a codebase that has never been linted?
hint: The full output is thousands of lines.

choices.text: `ruff check --diff`, which shows what a fix would change without changing it
choices.why: Useful and still thousands of lines on a first run.

choices.text: `ruff check --fix`, so the easy half is gone before anybody reads the list
choices.why: A large unreviewed rewrite is a poor first commit even when every fix is safe.

choices.text: `ruff check --select ALL`, so the size of the problem is known
choices.why: That turns on every family including the contradictory ones.

choices.text: `ruff check --statistics`
choices.why: A count per rule is twenty lines and tells you what kind of problem you have.

prompt: Six tools are named as living inside `ruff`. What did it do with them?
hint: Not a wrapper.

choices.text: Reimplemented their rules, which is why it runs over a large repository in under a second
choices.why: `flake8`, `isort`, `pyupgrade`, `pydocstyle`, `autoflake` and most of `pylint`.

choices.text: Vendored them, so each one still runs as its own process behind one command
choices.why: Six processes would be slower than the six tools were.

choices.text: Wrapped their command-line interfaces behind a single configuration file
choices.why: A shared config would not make it faster.

choices.text: Translated their configuration formats, leaving the checks to the originals
choices.why: The checks are its own.

prompt: What does `[*]` beside a rule code mean?
hint: It is about what may be done automatically.

choices.text: The rule was matched more than once in the file being reported
choices.why: Each occurrence is printed on its own.

choices.text: The rule is in the default set and needs no `select` entry
choices.why: Default membership is not marked in the output.

choices.text: The rule was turned on by an `extend-select` rather than by `select`
choices.why: The output does not say where a rule came from.

choices.text: The rule has a fix `ruff` considers safe
choices.why: Safe means it cannot change what the program does — removing an unused import, sorting imports.

prompt: A config says `select = ["B"]`. What is checked?
hint: Read the verb.

choices.text: Bugbear, and nothing else — `select` replaces the default rather than adding to it
choices.why: An unused import in the same file is reported by nothing, because `F` was turned off by that line.

choices.text: Bugbear plus the default set, since a family is added to what was already on
choices.why: Adding to the default is `extend-select`.

choices.text: Bugbear plus `F`, since undefined names can never be switched off
choices.why: Every rule including `F` can be switched off.

choices.text: Nothing, since a `select` naming one family is rejected as too narrow
choices.why: It is accepted and does exactly what it says.

prompt: The default rule set is `E4, E7, E9, F`. What does that leave out that matters most?
hint: One family holds the defects.

choices.text: `I`, so the imports are never sorted and every diff touches the block
choices.why: Unsorted imports are untidy rather than a defect.

choices.text: `B`, and with it the mutable default argument that shares state
choices.why: `def load_rates(path, cache={})` passes the default set and is a cache shared by every call the process makes.

choices.text: `E501`, so a file with very long lines passes without comment
choices.why: Line length belongs to the formatter and is deliberately left out.

choices.text: `UP`, so the codebase keeps syntax older than the version it runs on
choices.why: Old syntax still runs correctly.

prompt: Why does `"__init__.py" = ["F401"]` belong in `per-file-ignores` rather than as a `# noqa` on each line?
hint: Think about what is being described.

choices.text: It is a property of that kind of file rather than a mistake on a line
choices.why: A package's `__init__.py` imports names so others can import them from there, and each looks unused.

choices.text: `# noqa` does not work on an import statement, so the config is the only way
choices.why: It works on any line, imports included.

choices.text: `F401` cannot be silenced on a line, only for a whole file
choices.why: It can be silenced either way; the question is which says the right thing.

choices.text: A `# noqa` in `__init__.py` is removed by `--fix` along with the import
choices.why: `--fix` leaves a suppressed finding alone.

prompt: `import json  # noqa: E501`, where the actual finding on that line is `F401`. What happens?
hint: The code named has to match.

choices.text: Nothing is reported, since any `noqa` comment covers the line
choices.why: That is what a bare `# noqa` does, and this one names a code.

choices.text: The `F401` is reported
choices.why: A `noqa` with a code silences that code. A bare `# noqa` silences every rule on the line, including next year's.

choices.text: The line is skipped entirely, including by the formatter
choices.why: The formatter reads no `noqa` comments.

choices.text: `ruff` reports that the named code does not apply to this line
choices.why: `RUF100` reports an unused directive, and it has to be turned on.

prompt: The rule that reports a suppression comment whose reason has gone: `______`
hint: Three letters and three digits.

prompt: Both tools take `line-length`. What goes wrong if the two numbers differ?
hint: One wraps and one reports.

choices.text: Whichever runs last wins, so the result depends on the order in CI
choices.why: The formatter's output does not depend on the linter having run.

choices.text: The linter rewraps the lines the formatter wrote, and the two fight on every save
choices.why: `ruff check` rewrites nothing about line width.

choices.text: The formatter refuses to run, since it reads the linter's table as well
choices.why: Each reads its own table and neither checks the other.

choices.text: The formatter produces lines the linter complains about, on files nobody touched
choices.why: Set them to the same value, and then turn `E501` off anyway.

prompt: What does `target-version` decide, for each of the two tools?
hint: Two different things from one number.

choices.text: Which syntax the formatter is allowed to emit, and what the `UP` family suggests
choices.why: With `py312`, `Optional[int]` becomes `int | None` and `typing.List` becomes `list`.

choices.text: Which Python the tools are run under, since each spawns its own interpreter
choices.why: Both read files and neither runs your code.

choices.text: Which version of each of the two tools is installed, resolved from the value given
choices.why: Tool versions are pinned by whatever installs them.

choices.text: Which standard-library signatures the linter believes in when checking calls
choices.why: Neither tool checks calls against signatures; that is a type checker's work.

prompt: `select` is written in `[tool.ruff]` instead of `[tool.ruff.lint]`. What happens?
hint: It is not an error.

choices.text: `ruff` refuses to start until that table is corrected
choices.why: It starts and runs.

choices.text: The setting applies to the formatter as well, which then rejects it
choices.why: The formatter has its own table and reads nothing from this one.

choices.text: A deprecation warning, and the setting still applies
choices.why: Which is how it goes unnoticed: nothing fails and the outer table keeps working.

choices.text: The setting is ignored silently and the default rule set is used
choices.why: It is honoured, with a warning printed alongside.

prompt: Which of these belongs in `exclude`?
hint: Whose file is it?

choices.text: The test suite, which has its own conventions about asserts and fixtures
choices.why: Those are a `per-file-ignores` entry rather than an exclusion.

choices.text: A module with a long list of findings, until somebody has time for it
choices.why: That is the directory that stops being checked and never comes back.

choices.text: A package's `__init__.py`, whose imports are all reported as unused
choices.why: Also a `per-file-ignores` entry, naming `F401`.

choices.text: A directory of machine-written files, such as migrations or generated clients
choices.why: Everything else is yours, and a directory excluded because it is inconvenient never comes back.

prompt: Why does the configuration belong in `pyproject.toml` rather than in the command?
hint: Three places run these tools.

choices.text: Because a flag cannot express a rule family, only a single rule code
choices.why: `--select B` works on the command line.

choices.text: Because `pyproject.toml` is the only place a per-file table can be written
choices.why: The per-file table could live in a `ruff.toml`; the reason is agreement.

choices.text: Because both tools ignore command-line flags when a config file exists
choices.why: A flag overrides the file, which is part of the problem.

choices.text: So that the editor, the terminal and the pipeline all do the same thing
choices.why: A tool configured on one machine's command line is a green check in one place and a red one in the other.

prompt: Why does CI run `--check` rather than the formatter itself?
hint: Think about what a pipeline is allowed to do to a branch.

choices.text: Formatting in CI is slower than checking, since the files have to be written back
choices.why: Writing a few files is not what makes a pipeline slow.

choices.text: A pipeline has no write access to the repository, so a rewrite would fail anyway
choices.why: Many pipelines do have write access, which is what makes the restraint a choice.

choices.text: `--check` is the only mode that reports which files would change
choices.why: `--diff` reports that too, in more detail.

choices.text: It reports the disagreement and does not quietly commit a fix into somebody's branch
choices.why: `--check` rewrites nothing and exits non-zero, which is the whole of the review comment nobody has to write.

prompt: A pre-commit hook runs both tools. Why keep the CI check as well?
hint: Where does the hook live?

choices.text: A hook runs on staged files only, so a file committed with `-a` is missed
choices.why: It runs on the files being committed, which includes those.

choices.text: A hook's version of the tool is pinned and CI's is not, so they drift
choices.why: Both should be pinned, and that is an argument for pinning rather than for keeping the check.

choices.text: A hook lives on each person's machine, is easy to skip, and is missing on a new one
choices.why: CI is what is true. The hook is what is convenient.

choices.text: A hook cannot run the formatter, only the linter with `--fix`
choices.why: It runs both; the sample config has one entry for each.

prompt: What is the right order to adopt these tools in?
hint: Something has to be able to go red first.

choices.text: The formatter everywhere and its `--check` in CI, then the linter's defaults, then one family at a time
choices.why: Doing it the other way round produces four thousand findings and a team that turns the tool off.

choices.text: The pre-commit hook first, since it stops new problems arriving
choices.why: It stops them on the machines that have it installed.

choices.text: The linter with every family on, so the size of the problem is known from the start
choices.why: That is the four thousand findings, and `--select ALL` also turns on contradictory rules.

choices.text: The editor integration first, so the code improves before any pipeline is touched
choices.why: Then the repository is half formatted and nothing says so.

prompt: Why put the formatter's check before the linter's in the pipeline?
hint: Think about what an unformatted file reports.

choices.text: A merely unformatted file then fails on the sentence that says so
choices.why: Rather than on a list of `E` findings that are all consequences of the same thing.

choices.text: The linter reads the formatter's output, so it has to run second
choices.why: Each reads the files in the repository; neither reads the other's output.

choices.text: Running them the other way round applies fixes the formatter then undoes
choices.why: Neither step changes a file when `--check` is used.

choices.text: The formatter's check is faster, so a failing build fails sooner
choices.why: Both are fast, and the ordering argument is about which message is read.

prompt: What does format-on-save buy that a CI check does not?
hint: Think about the file you are editing right now.

choices.text: It applies the linter's safe fixes as well, which CI is not allowed to do
choices.why: Organising imports on save is a separate editor setting.

choices.text: The repository is already formatted, so the pipeline never has to say so
choices.why: A formatter you have to remember to run is one half the repository has not been through.

choices.text: It catches findings before they are committed, unlike a check that runs after
choices.why: Formatting produces no findings; that is the linter's half.

choices.text: It formats files the CI check is configured to exclude
choices.why: Both honour the same `exclude` list from `pyproject.toml`.

prompt: `def load_rates(path, cache={})`. When is the dictionary created?
hint: Think about what the `def` statement does.

choices.text: Once, when the `def` runs
choices.why: It is attached to the function object and lives as long as the process, shared by every caller including the tests.

choices.text: Once per call, which is why it works as a cache within one request
choices.why: Then it would empty between calls and cache nothing at all.

choices.text: Once per module import, so a reimport in a test gives a fresh one
choices.why: A module is imported once per process and the default would survive anyway.

choices.text: Lazily, on the first call that does not pass the argument
choices.why: It is built when the `def` is executed, before any call.

prompt: What is the fix for `B006` on `cache={}`?
hint: The default has to be something immutable.

choices.text: `cache=None`, and `if cache is None: cache = {}` as the first line of the body
choices.why: The sentinel is built once and the dictionary is built per call, which is what was meant.

choices.text: `cache=dict()`, which constructs a new one rather than reusing a literal
choices.why: It is still evaluated once at definition; the call happens there, not per invocation.

choices.text: `cache=frozenset()`, which cannot be mutated and so cannot accumulate
choices.why: A frozen set cannot hold the mapping the function needs.

choices.text: Moving the argument after a `*`, so it has to be passed by keyword
choices.why: That changes how it is called and leaves the shared object exactly where it was.

prompt: `except:` with nothing after it. What does it catch that `except Exception:` does not?
hint: Two of them are how a process stops.

choices.text: `SyntaxError`, which is raised while the module is being read
choices.why: A syntax error in the module never reaches a `try` inside it, and it is an `Exception` anyway.

choices.text: Errors raised inside a C extension, which do not inherit from `Exception`
choices.why: An extension raises ordinary Python exceptions.

choices.text: `GeneratorExit` alone, which is the only other `BaseException` subclass
choices.why: There are several, and the two that matter here are the ones that stop a process.

choices.text: `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`
choices.why: So Ctrl-C inside that block is swallowed, and the process cannot be stopped while it is in there.

prompt: `for i in range(3): out.append(lambda: i)` then `[f() for f in out]`. What comes back?
hint: The closures share something.

choices.why: They share the variable rather than its value, and the loop finished with it at `2`.

choices.text: `[0, 1, 2]`, since each lambda was built while `i` held a different value
choices.why: Each lambda reads `i` when it is called, not when it was built.

choices.text: `[None, None, None]`, since `i` is out of scope once the loop ends
choices.why: A loop variable in Python outlives the loop.

choices.text: A `NameError`, since `i` is not bound inside the lambda's own scope
choices.why: It resolves to the enclosing scope, which is the whole problem.

prompt: `def summarise(rows, type=None)` and a later line calls `type(x)`. What happens?
hint: The name was taken.

choices.text: A `NameError`, since the parameter hid the built-in without replacing it
choices.why: The parameter is bound; it is bound to `None`.

choices.text: Nothing — `type` is looked up in the builtins namespace before the locals
choices.why: Locals are looked up first, which is the rule this finding is about.

choices.text: `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable`, from the line that calls it
choices.why: Inside that function the built-in is unreachable, in a function that has not itself changed.

choices.text: The built-in is used, since a parameter does not shadow it at module level
choices.why: A parameter is a local name and local names win inside the function.

prompt: Which of these four findings is tidiness rather than a defect?
hint: Three of them will produce a wrong answer at run time.

choices.text: `B023` — a function that does not bind the loop variable
choices.why: Every closure in the list does the last iteration's work.

choices.text: `E722` — a bare `except` around a JSON read
choices.why: It swallows Ctrl-C and turns a `NameError` into an empty dictionary.

choices.text: `B006` — a mutable data structure as an argument default
choices.why: That is a cache shared by every call the process makes.

choices.text: `F401` — an import nobody uses
choices.why: Somebody deleted the code that used it. `--fix` removes the line and nothing else happens.

prompt: Predict the reformat: `d = {'a':1,'b':2}` on a line that fits. What does `black` produce?
hint: Two kinds of change, both mechanical.

choices.why: Double quotes, and a space after each colon. It fits, so it stays on one line.

choices.text: The same dictionary exploded one key per line with a trailing comma
choices.why: It explodes only what does not fit, or what carries a magic trailing comma.

choices.text: `d = dict(a=1, b=2)`, which is the form it prefers for string keys
choices.why: It never rewrites one construct into another.

choices.text: `d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}`, with the spacing fixed and the quotes left alone
choices.why: It normalises to double quotes as well.

prompt: Turn the formatter into a build step that changes nothing and fails: `ruff format --______ .`
hint: Five letters.

prompt: A team turns on a new rule family and gets four hundred findings. What is the reasonable next step?
hint: The family is already on.

choices.text: Run `--fix --unsafe-fixes` and review the result as one diff
choices.why: Unsafe fixes can change behaviour and four hundred of them is not a reviewable diff.

choices.text: Run `--statistics`, then fix or ignore rule by rule, in a pull request of its own
choices.why: One family per pull request is what keeps the diff reviewable and the tool switched on.

choices.text: Add the family to `ignore` until somebody has time to work through it
choices.why: Ignoring a family you have just selected leaves the config claiming something untrue.

choices.text: Exclude the directories with the most findings and keep the rest
choices.why: Those directories then stop being checked and never come back.

prompt: Why is `result.ok == True` becoming `result.ok` classed as an unsafe fix?
hint: The two are not the same test.

choices.text: They differ for anything whose `__eq__` is unusual — `1 == True` is true and `1` is not `True`
choices.why: Read an unsafe fix's diff before taking it; that is what the flag is for.

choices.text: `result.ok` may be `None`, which is falsy where `== True` would raise
choices.why: Comparing `None` to `True` raises nothing; it is simply false.

choices.text: The rewrite moves the comparison into the `if`, changing where an exception surfaces
choices.why: Both forms evaluate `result.ok` in the same place.

choices.text: `ruff` cannot tell whether `ok` is a property with a side effect
choices.why: Both forms read the attribute exactly once.

prompt: A repository has `# noqa` with no code on eleven lines. What is the argument for naming codes instead?
hint: Think about next year.

choices.text: A bare comment applies to the whole block rather than to one line
choices.why: It applies to its own line.

choices.text: A bare comment is rejected by `ruff` unless `--preview` is passed
choices.why: It is accepted and does what it says.

choices.text: A bare comment is slower to process, since every rule has to be checked against it
choices.why: The cost is not measurable and is not the argument.

choices.text: A bare comment also silences the rule that starts applying to that line later
choices.why: And `RUF100` can then report the ones whose reason has gone.

prompt: Which tool finds that a function returns the wrong value for an input nobody tried?
hint: Neither of this lesson's two.

choices.text: Neither of the two — that is a test's job, and lesson 16 is where that half lives
choices.why: A linter finds what a machine can see in the text, which is a specific and useful set and not this.

choices.text: The linter, if the `B` family and the simplification rules are both on
choices.why: Those describe shapes of code rather than the answers it produces.

choices.text: The formatter, since a rewrite that changed the answer would be reported
choices.why: A formatter never changes the answer and reports nothing.

choices.text: The linter with `--unsafe-fixes`, which evaluates the expressions it rewrites
choices.why: It evaluates nothing; unsafe means it cannot prove the rewrite is equivalent.

prompt: `select = ["E", "F", "B", "SIM", "UP", "I", "A"]` and `ignore = ["E501"]`. What is the effect of the second line?
hint: It subtracts from the first.

choices.text: Line-length findings are dropped and the rest of `E` stays on
choices.why: The formatter owns the line width, so a report about it is a report about its decision.

choices.text: The whole `E` family is dropped, since a code in `ignore` disables its prefix
choices.why: `ignore` takes codes and prefixes, and `E501` is one code.

choices.text: Lines longer than the limit are reported as warnings rather than errors
choices.why: `ruff` has no warning level for a selected rule; it is on or off.

choices.text: The formatter stops wrapping at the configured width
choices.why: The formatter reads its own settings and ignores the linter's table.

prompt: What is in `.git-blame-ignore-revs` and why?
hint: One commit, and what it did.

choices.text: The hash of the commit that reformatted everything, so `blame` looks past it
choices.why: Otherwise the history stops being usable on the day the tool was adopted.

choices.text: The hashes of every commit made by an automated fix, so that blame names a person
choices.why: The file is for commits that touched everything without changing anything.

choices.text: A list of branches whose commits should not be blamed, such as release branches
choices.why: It holds revisions rather than branches.

choices.text: The hash of the last release, so blame stops at the current cycle
choices.why: Blame would then be useless for anything older.

prompt: Two people disagree about where a long call should break. What does this lesson say to do?
hint: Neither of them is right.

choices.text: Run the formatter over the file and stop having the conversation at all
choices.why: There is no right answer to it, which is exactly why handing it to a program costs nothing.

choices.text: Write it out one argument per line, which is what most teams settle on
choices.why: That is a preference, and a preference is what the formatter removes.

choices.text: Add a rule to the linter so the repository has one answer on record
choices.why: The linter would then report on layout, which is the formatter's half.

choices.text: Follow whatever the surrounding file does, so the diff stays small
choices.why: Then the file's style is whatever its first author preferred.
